The objection targets the sweep proof of Lemma (i). Is the text's proof adequately written? It's quite sketchy but does sketch an induction. The objection claims inconsistency: totals summing to T-d yet each at most (T-d)/2 forces equality. Actually text says "their uncancelled totals add to T-d" — wait: "so their uncancelled totals add to T-d". Then "each of total length at most (T-d)/2 = (2^s -1)d". Hmm, if two arrays sum to T-d total, each at most (T-d)/2 forces both equal exactly (T-d)/2. That is indeed a suspicious claim. Unless "their uncancelled totals add to T-d" means both combined, and then claiming each at most half... that can only hold with equality. Is the equality true? T-d = (2^{s+1}-1)d - d = 2^{s+1}-2 d = 2(2^s -1)d. So (T-d)/2 = (2^s -1)d. The claim "each of total length at most (2^s-1)d" together with sum = T-d = 2(2^s-1)d forces each exactly (2^s-1)d. That is generally false — cancellation need not split evenly. So the argument as written is inconsistent/incorrect. Also "at most s column-blocks" and undefined terms. So the objection is substantively right: the induction step's premise is flawed.

Quote faithful: yes. Verdict: confirmed (the inference is invalid; the stated inequality combined with the stated sum forces equality which is not generally true, and the induction cannot proceed). Evidence kind: invalid_inference. Fatal: yes — Lemma (i) underpins the upper bound for all n.

Together these force each array to have total exactly (2^s - 1)d, an equality that the sweep-and-cancel procedure does not generally produce (the split of uncancelled portions between the two parity rows depends on the geometry of the columns, not just their sum). Hence the stated bound cannot both be the per-array bound and the combined bound, and the induction premise ('an array with at most s column-blocks and total at most (2^s-1)d') is unjustified. Moreover, 'arrays' and 'column-blocks' are never defined, and no argument shows cuts on these derived arrays correspond to legal splits of actual pieces. Lemma (i) is the sole engine of the all-n upper bound (Section 4), so the proof is incomplete/invalid as written."}
